Hasta aquí los bucles corregían dentro d: Up to here the loops corrected within fixed rules. This topic asks what happens when the rules change and the loop stops working. Ashby's answer uses only two things: an inequality, which says whether a variable is within its limits, and the probability of getting it right first time, that of the [[pe-probabilidad|complementary event]].
Your internal temperature is about 37 °C. You can be in the snow or in the desert, running or asleep, and it is still 37. If it falls below 35 or rises above 41, you die. That is: there is a quantity that has to stay within a narrow margin, and everything else is at its service.
Ashby llamó <strong>variables esenciales: Ashby called those quantities essential variables and the fact of keeping them within their limits homeostasis. The word had been coined by the physiologist Walter Cannon in 1926, and it means literally “staying the same”; what Ashby contributed was turning it into mathematics.
Y aquí viene el giro que hace interesant: And here comes the twist that makes the topic interesting. A thermostat keeps a variable within its limits, yes, but only while the world behaves as the thermostat expects. If you change its rules —if you swap its wires, for example— it will go on cheerfully correcting in the wrong direction until it burns the house down. It does not know how to adapt, only how to correct.
La pregunta de Ashby era precisamente es: Ashby's question was precisely that: what would a machine be like that, on having its rules changed, found a new way of surviving by itself? Not one that corrected better, but one that reorganised itself. He called that property ultrastability, and it is the central concept of his 1952 book, Design for a Brain.
Lo primero es distinguir dos cosas que s: The first thing is to distinguish two things that are often confused. A system has many variables, but only a few are essential: the ones that have to stay within a range or the game is over. The rest are means.
En un cuerpo, las esenciales son la temp: In a body, the essential ones are temperature, the pH of the blood, glucose, oxygen; heart rate, breathing or sweat are not, and precisely for that reason they can vary enormously: they are the levers with which the others are kept in place. A marathon runner triples their heart rate so that their temperature does not rise two degrees.
Esa asimetría es una herramienta de anál: That asymmetry is a very practical tool of analysis outside biology. Faced with any system, the useful question is not “what variables does it have?” but “which can it not afford to lose, and which is it prepared to sacrifice to keep them?”. A firm sacrifices margin so as not to lose liquidity; an ecosystem sacrifices individuals to preserve the population; an operating system closes programs so as not to run out of memory.

Read as: “a less than or equal to x of t, less than or equal to b, for every t”.

Put another way: the essential variable $x$ has to be inside the interval $[a, b]$ at all times, not on average. That is more demanding than it looks: a system that meets the average but goes outside once has failed. A body whose average temperature is splendid but that passed through 43 °C for a minute is dead all the same.

El termostato no sabe que las reglas han: The thermostat does not know the rules have changed; it only knows how to correct. An ultrastable system would detect that the temperature is going outside the limits and would try another configuration.
Solo si alguien ha añadido un segundo ni: Only if someone has added a second level that watches the limits. A simple thermostat does not have one: that is exactly what it lacks to be ultrastable.
En 1948, con material sobrante de la gue: In 1948, with war surplus material, Ashby built a device to prove that ultrastability could be manufactured. He called it the homeostat and it consisted of four identical units connected to each other, each with a needle that could move in a trough of water.
El diseño tiene dos niveles, y ese es to: The design has two levels, and that is the whole trick. At the first, the four needles influence one another according to some coefficients: it is an ordinary feedback system, and it may turn out stable or not depending on how those coefficients are set.
El segundo nivel es la idea genial. Si a: The second level is the brilliant idea. If some needle goes outside its range —if an essential variable goes beyond its limits— a mechanism called a uniselector is triggered that changes the coefficients at random. And it tries again. And if that does not work either, again. Until it hits on a configuration that holds.
Merece la pena apreciar lo raro de esa s: It is worth appreciating how strange that solution is: the machine does not compute which configuration suits it. It does not reason, does not optimise, does not learn in the usual sense. It only does two things: detect that it is dying and shuffle again. And that is enough for it to find by itself a way of surviving situations its builder had not foreseen. Ashby swapped the wires in front of his colleagues and the device, after several shuffles, stabilised again.
Cuatro variables se influyen entre sí co: Four variables influence one another with random coefficients. The dotted lines are the survival limits: if any goes outside, the system reshuffles the coefficients and tries again. Press “disturb” to knock it out of place, or “swap the wires” to change the rules of its world, as Ashby did.

La estrategia del homeostato —probar al: The homeostat's strategy —try at random and keep what survives— is exactly that of biological evolution, and also that of several optimisation algorithms used today when the problem is so tangled that it cannot be differentiated: simulated annealing, genetic algorithms, random search. All share Ashby's moral: when you do not know what to do, it is enough to know how to recognise when things are going badly and to have a way of trying again.
Conviene separar bien los dos niveles, p: It is worth separating the two levels clearly, because it is the conceptual contribution of the topic.
cambiar las reglas cuando el primero fra: changing the rules when the first fails
Lo esencial es que el segundo nivel <str: The essential thing is that the second level only comes into action when the first has failed. While the essential variables are within their limits, nothing happens; the system does not go around changing strategy for the sake of it. The signal that triggers the reorganisation is not “this could be improved” but “this is killing me”.
Ese diseño en dos niveles se copia a men: That two-level design is often copied, although it is not called that. A computer system with automatic restart has exactly that architecture: while the metrics are within range, the service corrects itself; when they go outside, a supervisor restarts it with another configuration. In management it is called “management by exception”: not touching what works and reserving attention for what goes outside the limits, which is the only way for a regulator with little variety to govern something large.
Ashby presentó el homeostato en 1952 y p: Ashby presented the homeostat in 1952 and provoked a notable discussion. Grey Walter, another British pioneer who at the time was building robot tortoises that sought the light, praised it; others dismissed it saying that this was not intelligence but a device that drew numbers at random. Ashby replied with a question that is still a good one: if a mechanism survives a world it was not designed for, what more is being asked of it to call it adaptive? The discussion, in other words, is still alive today in every debate about what counts as intelligence in a machine.

El homeostato prueba configuraciones has: The homeostat tries configurations until it hits on a good one, so it is worth knowing how long that takes. The answer is simpler than it looks and no new formula is needed: thinking it through the right way round is enough.
Supón que de cada cinco configuraciones: Suppose that of every five configurations there is one that holds, that is, that the probability of succeeding in one draw is $p = 1/5$. If you make a hundred draws, you expect about twenty successes, spread more or less evenly over the hundred. Between one success and the next there are therefore about five draws. That is the average number of attempts until the first success: five, which is precisely $1/p$.

Se lee: <em>«los intentos de media son u:
Read as: “the attempts on average are one over p”, where $p$ is the probability of succeeding at each attempt.

With an everyday example: if a die gives a 6 with probability $1/6$, it has to be rolled six times on average to get the first 6. Not exactly six —it may come up first time or take twenty— but six on average if you repeat the experiment many times.

This situation, counting attempts until the first success, is called by the books the geometric distribution; here the name is not needed, only the reasoning above.
Este cálculo pone número al punto débil: This computation puts a number on the weak point of the method. The fewer configurations that work, the longer it takes, and the arithmetic gets worse fast: with twelve variables coupled in pairs there are millions of millions of possible combinations, and drawing blind would stop being viable. That is why Ashby's homeostat had four units and not forty, and why present-day methods that inherit his idea —genetic algorithms, simulated annealing— do not draw entirely blind: they keep what was working and only alter part of it.
